title: Thoughts on Legal Writing from Joseph M. Williams, Part I (NYSBA)
move: Nominalisation to verb: find the main characters, find the nominalisations naming their actions, turn them into verbs, make the characters the subjects.
before: The intention of the committee is to improve morale.
after: The committee intends to improve morale.
why: Williams's three-step procedure (analyse, assess, rewrite). Secondary summary of Williams, not the book.

title: Thoughts on Legal Writing from Joseph M. Williams, Part I (NYSBA)
move: Exceptions to nominalisation and passive rewrites: keep the noun when it is familiar or when the verb form reads worse; keep the passive when the old/known item should open the sentence.
before: I do not know what she intends. / The voters reelected the president with 54% of the vote.
after: I do not know her intentions. / The president was reelected with 54% of the vote.
why: Williams's rule is old information first, new and complex last ("start a sentence with old and simple information and end it with the new and complex"). Rules are defaults, not bans.

title: Sentence Clarity: Characters and Actions (Boston University)
move: Mechanical diagnostic: highlight every verb and underline its subject; highlight every to-be/to-have verb; underline nouns that could be verbs; rewrite with short concrete subjects and active verbs near the sentence start; add because/if/how to reconnect clauses. No before/after pairs on the page.
why: Gives an order of operations a reviser can run on a draft; the conjunction step restores the logic that nominalising hid.

title: Politics and the English Language (Orwell)
move: Six rules: no figure of speech you are used to seeing in print; short word over long; cut any word that can go; active over passive; everyday English over foreign, scientific or jargon words; break any rule before saying something outright barbarous. Rule 6 is the escape hatch.
before: I returned and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong (Ecclesiastes, quoted by Orwell)
after: Orwell's mock-modern version opens: Objective considerations of contemporary phenomena compel the conclusion that success or failure in competitive activities ... (fetch summary truncated its ending; check the essay for the full sentence)
why: Orwell's point: concrete images (race, battle) dissolve into abstraction that takes more syllables to say less. Names stale metaphors (toe the line, ride roughshod over) and pretentious diction (phenomenon, element, individual, objective, effective, basic) as targets.

title: GOV.UK A to Z style guide
move: Replace buzzword verbs by saying what is actually being done; delete empty connectives.
before: deliver (abstract) / drive (a scheme) / robust / utilise / going forward / in order to
after: make, create, provide or a more specific term / create, cause, encourage / well thought out, comprehensive / use / from now on, in the future / usually not needed, drop it
why: The guide: "With all of these words you can generally replace them by breaking the term into what you're actually doing." Also advises avoiding metaphors because they slow comprehension. A published house list is a ready-made grep for abstract-verb padding.

title: Exorcising the curse of knowledge (Harvard Gazette, on Pinker)
move: Curse-of-knowledge check: show the draft to a representative reader and revise where they stumble; do not assume your own sense of clarity is reliable. Cut compulsive hedges (somewhat, comparatively, to a certain degree); readers fill in the missing hedges themselves.
why: Pinker defines the curse as the failure to understand that other people don't know what we know, and says abstract language is not needed just because the concept is hard. No before/after pairs in the article.

title: The Curse of Knowledge (APS Observer)
move: Empathy is not enough to beat the curse of knowledge; test the draft on a real reader.

title: Zombie nouns and verbs (Andy Naselli, quoting Pinker pp. 50-52)
move: Zombie noun repair: turn the -ance/-ation/-ing noun back into its verb.
before: (Pinker's wording per the post) a spry verb embalmed into a lifeless noun
after: John emphasizes faith (as the stronger form, per the search summary)
why: Term is Helen Sword's; Pinker adopts it. Second-hand; no full before sentence seen.

title: Nature review of The Sense of Style
move: Do not ban the passive: it lets the writer direct the reader's gaze like a camera angle, and it can omit the agent. Pinker also faults Strunk and White for appealing to the writer's ear instead of rules that can be applied.
why: Snippet via search summary only; supports a conditional rule: choose passive when the patient is the topic, not by blanket rule.

title: Language Log on Pullum and Strunk & White
move: Passive is the normal choice when the actor is unknown or unimportant or when a new subject is being introduced; a blanket rule against it mislabels weak active sentences as passive.
why: Snippet only. Pullum's original (Chronicle, 2009) returned 403; Cambridge PDF unreadable. Counts of misidentified passives not verified.

title: How I edit AI-generated copy and why it takes so long (Wondering About AI)
move: Editor's order for AI drafts (SHARP): (1) verify or cut unsupported stats, names, quotes, citations; (2) cut em-dashes, stock transitions, false contrasts, explainer verbs, repeated urgency words and rewrite in the writer's voice; (3) add what a model can't generate (firsthand experience, comparisons, real quotes); (4) read aloud for pacing; (5) rest and re-judge.
before: The problem? Integration complexity. / It's not about having more data, it's about having the right data. / Let's dive deep into why customer retention metrics matter. / Marketing automation helps teams scale their efforts — saving time and resources —
after: Integration complexity blocks progress. / The right data matters more than simply having a lot of it. / Customer retention metrics matter because they predict revenue. / Marketing automation helps teams scale their efforts and save resources while maintaining personalization.
why: Before/after pairs come from the Proofed checklist as relayed by this page's fetch summary; the Proofed page itself returned truncated content. Names an editor-ish blogger, not a famous working editor.

title: AI Editing Checklist (Proofed)
move: Replace every category noun with a real instance; add a number, name, date or detail from the writer's own week; cut the warm generic closing summary and end on the sharpest specific line or the actual ask.
why: Professional editing company; page fetched truncated, so moves come from search summary only. Em-dash thresholds vary by guide (2 per 1,000 words; 1 per 200 as a flag), so treat as a diagnostic, not a rule: swapping the dash for a hyphen does not fix the rhythm.

title: A Humanizer Should Not Become a House Style Manual (Drop Times)
move: Warning: a checklist of AI tells (rule of three, etc.) can harden into one house style; the goal is restoring a particular writer's voice, not avoiding a pattern list.
why: Snippet only; rule-of-three as an AI tell is weakly sourced in everything seen.

title: Sentence rhythm (Provost, 100 Ways to Improve Your Writing, via Lumen)
move: Vary sentence length: a run of same-length short sentences reads as a drone; mix short, medium and long, with a long sentence that builds then a short one for emphasis.
before: A run of five-word sentences (Provost's demonstration)
after: Short, medium and long sentences mixed, which Provost says gives the prose a lilt
why: Provost's own passage was not reproduced or read in full; secondary citations only (book 1985, p. 61 per one citation).
